claim: A larval brain lobe contains approximately 100 neuroblasts.
source: A larval brain lobe contains approximately 100 neuroblasts, and each neuroblast asymmetrically divides every 60–90 min, regenerating itself and producing a sibling progeny that commits to generating differentiated cell types.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the number of neuroblasts in a larval brain lobe.

claim: Each neuroblast asymmetrically divides every 60–90 min.
source: A larval brain lobe contains approximately 100 neuroblasts, and each neuroblast asymmetrically divides every 60–90 min, regenerating itself and producing a sibling progeny that commits to generating differentiated cell types.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the division frequency of neuroblasts.

claim: Most neuroblasts in the larval brain are type I.
source: Most of these neuroblasts are type I, which generate a ganglion mother cell (GMC) in every division.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the predominant type of neuroblasts.

claim: Type I neuroblasts generate a ganglion mother cell (GMC) in every division.
source: Most of these neuroblasts are type I, which generate a ganglion mother cell (GMC) in every division.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the progeny of type I neuroblasts.

claim: A GMC undergoes terminal division to produce two neurons.
source: A GMC undergoes terminal division to produce two neurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about GMC division.

claim: Eight neuroblasts are type II.
source: Eight neuroblasts are type II, which invariably generate an immature intermediate neural progenitor (immature INP) in every division (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Type II neuroblasts invariably generate an immature intermediate neural progenitor (immature INP) in every division.
source: Eight neuroblasts are type II, which invariably generate an immature intermediate neural progenitor (immature INP) in every division (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: An immature INP initiates INP commitment 60 min after asymmetric neuroblast division.
source: An immature INP initiates INP commitment 60 min after asymmetric neuroblast division (Janssens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: An immature INP initially lacks Asense (Ase) protein expression.
source: An immature INP initially lacks Asense (Ase) protein expression and upregulates Ase as it progresses through INP commitment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Ase expression in immature INPs.

claim: An immature INP upregulates Ase as it progresses through INP commitment.
source: An immature INP initially lacks Asense (Ase) protein expression and upregulates Ase as it progresses through INP commitment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Ase expression dynamics.

claim: Once INP commitment is complete, an Ase+ immature INP transitions into an INP.
source: Once INP commitment is complete, an Ase+ immature INP transitions into an INP and asymmetrically divides 5–6 times to generate more than a dozen differentiated cells, including neurons and glia (Viktorin et al., 2011; Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: An INP asymmetrically divides 5–6 times to generate more than a dozen differentiated cells, including neurons and glia.
source: Once INP commitment is complete, an Ase+ immature INP transitions into an INP and asymmetrically divides 5–6 times to generate more than a dozen differentiated cells, including neurons and glia (Viktorin et al., 2011; Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: All type II neuroblast lineage cell types in larval brains can be unambiguously identified based on functional characteristics and protein marker expression.
source: All type II neuroblast lineage cell types in larval brains can be unambiguously identified based on functional characteristics and protein marker expression.
evidence: This is a direct statement about cell type identification.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) of sorted, fluorescently labeled INPs and their differentiating progeny from wild-type brain tissue has led to the discovery of many new genes that contribute to the generation of diverse differentiated cell types during neurogenesis.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) of sorted, fluorescently labeled INPs and their differentiating progeny from wild-type brain tissue has led to the discovery of many new genes that contribute to the generation of diverse differentiated cell types during neurogenesis (Michki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: Activated Notch signaling drives the expression of downstream-effector genes deadpan (dpn) and Enhancer of (splitz)mγ (E(spl)mγ).
source: Activated Notch signaling drives the expression of downstream-effector genes deadpan (dpn) and Enhancer of (splitz)mγ (E(spl)mγ), which promote stemness in type II neuroblasts by poising activation of the master regulator of INP commitment earmuff (erm) (San-Juán and Baonza, 2011; Xiao et al., 2012; Zacharioudaki et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2012; Zacharioudaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: dpn and E(spl)mγ promote stemness in type II neuroblasts by poising activation of the master regulator of INP commitment earmuff (erm).
source: Activated Notch signaling drives the expression of downstream-effector genes deadpan (dpn) and Enhancer of (splitz)mγ (E(spl)mγ), which promote stemness in type II neuroblasts by poising activation of the master regulator of INP commitment earmuff (erm) (San-Juán and Baonza, 2011; Xiao et al., 2012; Zacharioudaki et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2012; Zacharioudaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: During asymmetric neuroblast division, the basal protein Numb and Brain tumor (Brat) exclusively segregate into immature INPs.
source: During asymmetric neuroblast division, the basal protein Numb and Brain tumor (Brat) exclusively segregate into immature INPs, where they terminate Notch signaling activity and promote the timely onset of Erm expression (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006a; Lee et al., 2006b; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Numb and Brat terminate Notch signaling activity and promote the timely onset of Erm expression in immature INPs.
source: During asymmetric neuroblast division, the basal protein Numb and Brain tumor (Brat) exclusively segregate into immature INPs, where they terminate Notch signaling activity and promote the timely onset of Erm expression (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006a; Lee et al., 2006b; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Numb is a conserved Notch inhibitor and prevents continual Notch activation in immature INPs.
source: Numb is a conserved Notch inhibitor and prevents continual Notch activation in immature INPs (Frise et al., 1996; Zhong et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2006a; Wang et al., 2006; Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Asymmetric segregation of the RNA-binding protein Brat is facilitated by its adapter protein Miranda.
source: Asymmetric segregation of the RNA-binding protein Brat is facilitated by its adapter protein Miranda, which releases Brat from the cortex of immature INPs, allowing Brat to promote decay of Notch downstream-effector gene transcripts and thus initiate differentiation (Loedige et al., 2014; Laver et al., 2015; Loedige et al., 2015; Komori et al., 2018; Reichardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Miranda releases Brat from the cortex of immature INPs, allowing Brat to promote decay of Notch downstream-effector gene transcripts and thus initiate differentiation.
source: Asymmetric segregation of the RNA-binding protein Brat is facilitated by its adapter protein Miranda, which releases Brat from the cortex of immature INPs, allowing Brat to promote decay of Notch downstream-effector gene transcripts and thus initiate differentiation (Loedige et al., 2014; Laver et al., 2015; Loedige et al., 2015; Komori et al., 2018; Reichardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Complete loss of numb or brat function leads to unrestrained activation of Notch signaling in immature INPs driving them to revert into type II neuroblasts leading to a severe supernumerary neuroblast phenotype.
source: Complete loss of numb or brat function leads to unrestrained activation of Notch signaling in immature INPs driving them to revert into type II neuroblasts leading to a severe supernumerary neuroblast phenotype.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype resulting from loss of numb or brat.

claim: Increased levels of activated Notch or Notch transcriptional target gene expression in immature INPs can drastically enhance the moderate supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in brat- or numb-hypomorphic brains.
source: Similarly, increased levels of activated Notch or Notch transcriptional target gene expression in immature INPs can drastically enhance the moderate supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in brat- or numb-hypomorphic brains (Xiao et al., 2012; Janssens et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014b; Komori et al., 2018; Larson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Precise transcriptional control of Notch and Notch target gene expression levels during asymmetric neuroblast division is essential, safeguarding the generation of neurons that are required for neuronal circuit formation in adult brains.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that precise transcriptional control of Notch and Notch target gene expression levels during asymmetric neuroblast division is essential, safeguarding the generation of neurons that are required for neuronal circuit formation in adult brains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings presented.

claim: fruitless (fru) mRNAs are detected in type I & II neuroblasts but not in their differentiating progeny.
source: From a type II neuroblast lineage-specific single-cell gene transcriptomic atlas, we found that fruitless (fru) mRNAs are detected in type I & II neuroblasts but not in their differentiating progeny.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on scRNA-seq data.

claim: One specific Zn-finger containing isoform of Fru (FruC) is exclusively expressed in all neuroblasts.
source: One specific Zn-finger containing isoform of Fru (FruC) is exclusively expressed in all neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a direct statement about FruC expression.

claim: FruC binds cis-regulatory elements of most genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts, including Notch and Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts.
source: FruC binds cis-regulatory elements of most genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts, including Notch and Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data.

claim: A modest increase in Notch or Notch downstream gene expression induced by loss of fruC function alone has no effect on INP commitment.
source: A modest increase in Notch or Notch downstream gene expression induced by loss of fruC function alone has no effect on INP commitment, but enhances immature INP reversion to type II neuroblasts in numb- and brat-hypomorphic brains.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results.

claim: Loss of fruC function enhances immature INP reversion to type II neuroblasts in numb- and brat-hypomorphic brains.
source: A modest increase in Notch or Notch downstream gene expression induced by loss of fruC function alone has no effect on INP commitment, but enhances immature INP reversion to type II neuroblasts in numb- and brat-hypomorphic brains.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results.

claim: FruC-dependent low-level enrichment of the repressive histone marker H3K27me3 occurs in most FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts including Notch and its downstream-effector genes.
source: We surprisingly found FruC-dependent low-level enrichment of the repressive histone marker H3K27me3 in most FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts including Notch and its downstream-effector genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data.

claim: The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) subunits are enriched in FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts.
source: The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) subunits are enriched in FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts, and reduced PRC2 function enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numb-hypomorphic brains, identical to fruC loss-of-function.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data.

claim: Reduced PRC2 function enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numb-hypomorphic brains, identical to fruC loss-of-function.
source: The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) subunits are enriched in FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts, and reduced PRC2 function enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numb-hypomorphic brains, identical to fruC loss-of-function.
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results.

claim: The FruC-PRC2-H3K27me3 molecular pathway fine-tunes stemness gene expression in neuroblasts by promoting low-level H3K27me3 enrichment in their cis-regulatory elements.
source: We conclude that the FruC-PRC2-H3K27me3 molecular pathway fine-tunes stemness gene expression in neuroblasts by promoting low-level H3K27me3 enrichment in their cis-regulatory elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The mechanism by which PRC2-H3K27me3 fine-tune stem cell gene expression will likely be relevant throughout metazoans.
source: The mechanism by which PRC2-H3K27me3 fine-tune stem cell gene expression will likely be relevant throughout metazoans.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader relevance of the findings.

claim: The harmonized scRNA-seq dataset captures molecularly and functionally defined stages of differentiation in the type II neuroblast lineage.
source: Thus, the harmonized scRNA-seq dataset captures molecularly and functionally defined stages of differentiation in the type II neuroblast lineage (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the scRNA-seq data and Figure 1F.

claim: Cluster 14 contains type II neuroblasts (dpn+,erm-,ase-,ham-), Ase- immature INPs (dpn-,erm+,ase-,ham-) and Ase+ immature INPs (dpn-,erm-,ase+,ham+).
source: We found that cluster 14 contains type II neuroblasts (dpn+,erm-,ase-,ham-), Ase- immature INPs (dpn-,erm+,ase-,ham-) and Ase+ immature INPs (dpn-,erm-,ase+,ham+) (Figure 1E), which are well-defined rapidly changing transcriptional states during INP commitment (Xiao et al., 2012; Janssens et al., 2014; Rives-Quinto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on scRNA-seq data and Figure 1E, supported by citations.

claim: Cluster 1 contains proliferating INPs that express known differential temporal transcription factors, including young INPs (D+,hbn-,ey-,scro-) and old INPs (D-,hbn+,ey+,scro+).
source: Furthermore, cluster 1 contains proliferating INPs that express known differential temporal transcription factors (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Tang et al., 2022), including young INPs (D+,hbn-,ey-,scro-) and old INPs (D-,hbn+,ey+,scro+) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on scRNA-seq data and Figure 1E, supported by citations.

claim: The type II neuroblast lineage gene transcription atlas captures neuroblast progeny undergoing dynamic changes in cell identity during differentiation.
source: These data led us to conclude that the type II neuroblast lineage gene transcription atlas captures neuroblast progeny undergoing dynamic changes in cell identity during differentiation (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the scRNA-seq data and Figure 1F.

claim: fru transcripts are highly enriched in type II neuroblasts but lower in Ase- immature INPs.
source: We found the expression of fru mirrors dpn expression, with transcript levels high in type II neuroblasts but lower in Ase- immature INPs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on scRNA-seq data and Figure 2A.

claim: fru is a pleiotropic gene with at least two major functions: one that controls male sexual behavior and another that is essential for viability in both sexes.
source: fru is a pleiotropic gene with at least two major functions: one that controls male sexual behavior and another that is essential for viability in both sexes (Goodwin and Hobert, 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: fru transcripts are alternatively spliced into multiple isoforms that encode putative transcription factors containing a common BTB (protein-protein interaction) N-terminal domain and one of four C-terminal zinc-finger DNA-binding domains.
source: fru transcripts are alternatively spliced into multiple isoforms that encode putative transcription factors containing a common BTB (protein-protein interaction) N-terminal domain and one of four C-terminal zinc-finger DNA-binding domains (Dalton et al., 2013; Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations and Figure 2A.

claim: Fru is detected in neuroblasts but rapidly downregulated in their differentiating progeny in type I and II lineages.
source: We detected Fru in neuroblasts but found that Fru is rapidly downregulated in their differentiating progeny in type I and II lineages (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on immunofluorescence data and Figure 2B.

claim: FruC::Myc is specifically expressed in both types of neuroblasts but not in their differentiating progeny, including immature INPs, INPs, and GMCs.
source: While FruA::Myc and FruB::Myc appear to be ubiquitously expressed at low levels, FruC::Myc is specifically expressed in both types of neuroblasts but not in their differentiating progeny, including immature INPs, INPs, and GMCs (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on immunofluorescence data and Figures 2C and 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: FruC is the predominant Fru isoform expressed in neuroblasts.
source: These data indicate that FruC is the predominant Fru isoform expressed in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression data.

claim: The wild-type neuroblast clone always contains a single neuroblast that can be uniquely identified by cell size (10–12 μm in diameter) and marker expression (Dpn+Ase-).
source: The wild-type neuroblast clone always contains a single neuroblast that can be uniquely identified by cell size (10–12 μm in diameter) and marker expression (Dpn+Ase-) as well as 6–8 smaller, Dpn- immature INPs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on clonal analysis and Figure 2D.

claim: The neuroblast clone carrying deletion of the fru locus (fru-/-) contains a single identifiable neuroblast but frequently contains multiple Ase- immature INPs with detectable Dpn expression.
source: The neuroblast clone carrying deletion of the fru locus (fru-/-) contains a single identifiable neuroblast but frequently contains multiple Ase- immature INPs with detectable Dpn expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on clonal analysis and Figure 2E.

claim: Over 80% of newborn immature INPs (marked by intense cortical Mira expression) generated by fruC-mutant type II neuroblasts ectopically express Dpn and E(spl)mγ.
source: Over 80% of newborn immature INPs (marked by intense cortical Mira expression) generated by fruC-mutant type II neuroblasts ectopically express Dpn and E(spl)mγ while less than 15% of newborn immature INPs generated by wild-type neuroblasts expressed these genes (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on immunofluorescence data and Figures 2F–I.

claim: Less than 15% of newborn immature INPs generated by wild-type neuroblasts express Dpn and E(spl)mγ.
source: Over 80% of newborn immature INPs (marked by intense cortical Mira expression) generated by fruC-mutant type II neuroblasts ectopically express Dpn and E(spl)mγ while less than 15% of newborn immature INPs generated by wild-type neuroblasts expressed these genes (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on immunofluorescence data and Figures 2F–I.

claim: Loss of fruC function increases the expression of Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts.
source: These results support a model in which loss of fruC function increases the expression of Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Type II neuroblasts overexpressing FruC prematurely initiate INP commitment, as indicated by a reduced cell diameter and precocious Ase expression.
source: Consistently, type II neuroblasts overexpressing FruC prematurely initiate INP commitment, as indicated by a reduced cell diameter and precocious Ase expression (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 2J–L.

claim: Loss of fruC function increases stemness gene expression whereas gain of fruC decreases stemness gene expression during asymmetric neuroblast division.
source: Thus, loss of fruC function increases stemness gene expression whereas gain of fruC decreases stemness gene expression during asymmetric neuroblast division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Ectopic translation of Notch downstream-effector gene transcripts that promote stemness in neuroblasts drives immature INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts at the expense of differentiating cell types in brat-null brains.
source: Ectopic translation of Notch downstream-effector gene transcripts that promote stemness in neuroblasts drives immature INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts at the expense of differentiating cell types in brat-null brains (Loedige et al., 2015; Komori et al., 2018; Reichardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: Control clones in brat-null brains contain mostly type II neuroblasts and few differentiating cells that include Ase+ immature INPs, INPs, and GMCs.
source: Control clones in brat-null brains contain mostly type II neuroblasts and few differentiating cells that include Ase+ immature INPs, INPs, and GMCs (Figure 2M and P).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on clonal analysis and Figures 2M and P.

claim: Overexpressing full-length FruC increases the number of INPs, GMCs, and differentiating neurons (Ase-Pros+) in brat-null neuroblast clones.
source: By contrast, overexpressing full-length FruC increases the number of INPs, GMCs, and differentiating neurons (Ase-Pros+) in brat-null neuroblast clones (Figure 2N and P).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on clonal analysis and Figures 2N and P.

claim: FruC overexpression is sufficient to partially restore differentiation in brat-null brains.
source: This result indicates that FruC overexpression is sufficient to partially restore differentiation in brat-null brains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Overexpressing FruC,zf::ERD was sufficient to partially restore differentiation in brat-null brains.
source: Similar to full-length FruC overexpression, overexpressing FruC,zf::ERD was also sufficient to partially restore differentiation in brat-null brains (Figure 2O–P).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 2O–P.

claim: FruC negatively regulates stemness gene expression in type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, we conclude that FruC negatively regulates stemness gene expression in type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: FruC binds 9301 regions in type II neuroblasts.
source: FruC binds 9301 regions in type II neuroblasts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 3A.

claim: 59% of FruC-bound regions are promoters whereas 29% are enhancers in the intergenic and intronic regions.
source: Overall, 59% of FruC-bound regions are promoters whereas 29% are enhancers in the intergenic and intronic regions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 3A.

claim: 15% of randomized control regions are promoters and 55% are enhancers.
source: By contrast, 15% of randomized control regions are promoters and 55% are enhancers (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on analysis of randomized control regions and Figure 3A.

claim: 50.1% of FruC-bound regions in promoters and enhancers overlap with regions of accessible chromatin.
source: 50.1% of FruC-bound regions in promoters and enhancers overlap with regions of accessible chromatin (Larson et al., 2021; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq data, supported by a citation and Figure 3B.

claim: FruC binds promoters and neuroblast-specific enhancers of Notch, dpn, E(spl)mγ, klumpfuss (klu) and tailless (tll).
source: Consistent with the finding that FruC negatively regulates stemness gene expression, FruC binds promoters and neuroblast-specific enhancers of Notch, dpn, E(spl)mγ, klumpfuss (klu) and tailless (tll) that were previously shown to maintain type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 3C and 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Seventy-four percent of genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts (NB genes) are bound by FruC whereas 41% of these genes are in randomized control.
source: Seventy-four percent of genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts (NB genes) are bound by FruC whereas 41% of these genes are in randomized control (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN and scRNA-seq data and Figures 3D–E.

claim: The percentage of FruC-bound genes transcribed in immature INPs or throughout the type II neuroblast lineage is similar to random control.
source: By contrast, the percentage of FruC-bound genes transcribed in immature INPs or throughout the type II neuroblast lineage is similar to random control (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN and scRNA-seq data and Figures 3D–E.

claim: FruC preferentially binds cis-regulatory elements of stemness genes.
source: Because stemness gene transcripts are highly enriched in type II neuroblasts, these results suggest that FruC preferentially binds cis-regulatory elements of stemness genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Su(H) binds 305 regions in 112 genes in type II neuroblasts.
source: We found that Su(H) binds 305 regions in 112 genes in type II neuroblasts, and that Su(H)-bound regions are predominantly in promoters and enhancers (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 3F.

claim: Su(H)-bound regions are predominantly in promoters and enhancers.
source: We found that Su(H) binds 305 regions in 112 genes in type II neuroblasts, and that Su(H)-bound regions are predominantly in promoters and enhancers (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 3F.

claim: Twelve percent of NB genes are bound by Su(H) compared to 0% of these gene in a randomized control.
source: Twelve percent of NB genes are bound by Su(H) compared to 0% of these gene in a randomized control (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN and scRNA-seq data and Figures 3D–E.

claim: 95.2% of Su(H)-bound promoters and 90.8% of Su(H)-bound enhancers overlap with FruC-bound peaks.
source: Overall, 95.2% of Su(H)-bound promoters and 90.8% of Su(H)-bound enhancers overlap with FruC-bound peaks (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 3G.

claim: FruC regulates Notch pathway gene expression by occupying functionally relevant regulatory elements bound by Notch in type II neuroblasts.
source: Our data support a model that FruC regulates Notch pathway gene expression by occupying functionally relevant regulatory elements bound by Notch in type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: A sequence bound by the transcription factor Trithorax-like (Trl) is significantly enriched in both FruC-bound promoters and enhancers.
source: De novo motif discovery identified a sequence bound by the transcription factor Trithorax-like (Trl), also known as GAGA factor, is significantly enriched in both FruC-bound promoters and enhancers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on motif analysis and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The Trl motif was previously found to be the most significantly enriched in FruC-associated genomic regions in the larval nervous system.
source: The Trl motif was previously found to be the most significantly enriched in FruC-associated genomic regions in the larval nervous system (Neville et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: Trl is a member of the BTB-Zn-finger transcription factor family which heterodimerize with other BTB-domain-containing factors to regulate gene transcription.
source: Trl, like Fru, is a member of the BTB-Zn-finger transcription factor family which heterodimerize with other BTB-domain-containing factors to regulate gene transcription (Bonchuk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: Trl is an evolutionarily conserved multifaceted transcription factor that regulates diverse biological processes by interacting with a wide variety of proteins including PRC2 complex components.
source: Trl is an evolutionarily conserved multifaceted transcription factor that regulates diverse biological processes by interacting with a wide variety of proteins including PRC2 complex components (Lomaev et al., 2017; Chetverina et al., 2021; Srivastava et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: 85.4% of Trl-bound promoters and 87.8% of Trl-bound enhancers overlapped with FruC-bound regions including Notch, dpn, E(spl)mγ, klu and tll loci.
source: In total, 85.4% of Trl-bound promoters and 87.8% of Trl-bound enhancers overlapped with FruC-bound regions including Notch, dpn, E(spl)mγ, klu and tll loci (Figure 3C and I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 3C, 3I, and 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FruC may function together with Trl to regulate the transcription of stemness genes in neuroblasts.
source: These data suggest that FruC may function together with Trl to regulate the transcription of stemness genes in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: FruC likely fine-tunes Notch signaling activity levels that balance neuroblast maintenance and INP commitment during neuroblast asymmetric division.
source: Loss- and gain-of-function of fruC mildly alters the expression of Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts (Figure 2). Thus, FruC likely fine-tunes Notch signaling activity levels that balance neuroblast maintenance and INP commitment during neuroblast asymmetric division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Immature INPs revert to supernumerary type II neuroblasts at low frequency due to a modest increase in Notch downstream-effector gene expression in brathypo brains.
source: Immature INPs revert to supernumerary type II neuroblasts at low frequency due to a modest increase in Notch downstream-effector gene expression in brathypo brains (Komori et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: The heterozygosity of a fru deletion (fru-/+) enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in brathypo brains.
source: Consistent with the finding that reduced fru function increases Notch downstream-effector protein levels in immature INPs, the heterozygosity of a fru deletion (fru-/+) enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in brathypo brains (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 4A and 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: brathypo brains lacking fruC function displayed greater than a twofold increase in supernumerary neuroblasts compared with brathypo brains heterozygous for a fru deletion.
source: Furthermore, brathypo brains lacking fruC function displayed greater than a twofold increase in supernumerary neuroblasts compared with brathypo brains heterozygous for a fru deletion (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 4A and 4—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Loss of fruC function increases Notch pathway activity levels during asymmetric neuroblast division.
source: These data support our model that loss of fruC function increases Notch pathway activity levels during asymmetric neuroblast division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Overexpressing two copies of dominant-negative mam transgenes in immature INPs partially suppresses the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains.
source: Antagonizing Notch-activated gene transcription by overexpressing a dominant negative form of Mam (MamDN) in immature INPs suppressed the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains (Figure 4C–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 4C–D and 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains provides a direct functional readout of activated Notch levels during asymmetric neuroblast division.
source: Thus, the supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains provides a direct functional readout of activated Notch levels during asymmetric neuroblast division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The heterozygosity of a fru deletion alone did not affect INP commitment in immature INPs but led to a twofold increase in supernumerary neuroblasts in numbhypo brains.
source: The heterozygosity of a fru deletion alone did not affect INP commitment in immature INPs but led to a twofold increase in supernumerary neuroblasts in numbhypo brains (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 4E and 4—figure supplement 1H–I.

claim: Complete loss of fruC function (fru-/ΔC) led to increased supernumerary neuroblast formation in numbhypo brains compared with fru-/+.
source: Complete loss of fruC function (fru-/ΔC) led to increased supernumerary neuroblast formation in numbhypo brains compared with fru-/+ (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–L).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 4E and 4—figure supplement 1J–L.

claim: FruC fine-tunes the transcription of Notch downstream-effector genes in neuroblasts.
source: These results suggest that loss of fruC function increases Notch-activated gene expression in mitotic neuroblasts, and support a model that FruC fine-tunes the transcription of Notch downstream-effector genes in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The number of CycE nascent transcript foci in neuroblasts appears statistically indistinguishable between control brains carrying only the Gal4 driver or brains overexpressing fruCRNAi.
source: Consistently, the number of CycE nascent transcript foci in neuroblasts appears statistically indistinguishable between control brains carrying only the Gal4 driver or brains overexpressing fruCRNAi (Figure 4F–G and O).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on sm-FISH data and Figures 4F–G and O.

claim: The number of Notch, dpn and klu nascent transcript foci is significantly higher in fruC knockdown brains than in control brains.
source: By contrast, the number of Notch, dpn and klu nascent transcript foci is significantly higher in fruC knockdown brains than in control brains (Figure 4H–O).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on sm-FISH data and Figures 4H–O.

claim: Reduced fruC function increases Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene transcription levels in neuroblasts.
source: These results strongly suggest that reduced fruC function increases Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene transcription levels in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sm-FISH data.

claim: Knocking down the function of E(spl)mγ by RNAi strongly suppressed increased supernumerary neuroblast formation in numbhypo brains heterozygous for fru while not effecting the baseline supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, knocking down the function of E(spl)mγ by RNAi strongly suppressed increased supernumerary neuroblast formation in numbhypo brains heterozygous for fru while not effecting the baseline supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains (Figure 4P).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figure 4P.

claim: Reducing fruC function increases Notch target gene transcription in neuroblasts.
source: This result provides functional support of our model that reducing fruC function increases Notch target gene transcription in neuroblasts. Thus, we conclude that FruC fine-tunes Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene expression during asymmetric neuroblast division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: 14.2% (4139 kB / 29,065 kB) of the regions with statistically significant changes in H3K27ac levels genome-wide displayed greater than twofold increase in this histone mark in fruC-null brains while 0.4% (130 kB / 29,065 kB) of these regions showed greater than twofold decrease.
source: 14.2% (4139 kB / 29,065 kB) of the regions with statistically significant changes in H3K27ac levels genome-wide displayed greater than twofold increase in this histone mark in fruC-null brains while 0.4% (130 kB / 29,065 kB) of these regions showed greater than twofold decrease (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 3.4% (306 kB / 8,870 kB) of FruC-bound regions showed greater than 2-fold increase in H3K27ac levels in fruC-null brains.
source: 3.4% (306 kB / 8,870 kB) of FruC-bound regions showed greater than 2-fold increase in H3K27ac levels in fruC-null brains, and these regions did not include the cis-regulatory elements and the bodies of Notch, dpn and E(spl)mγ (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 5A and 5—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Loss of fruC function did not significantly increase the number of FruC-bound loci with greater than 2-fold increase in H3K27ac comparing with the genome overall.
source: Thus, loss of fruC function did not significantly increase the number of FruC-bound loci with greater than 2-fold increase in H3K27ac comparing with the genome overall.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: H3K27 deacetylation likely plays a minor role in FruC-mediated fine-tuning of target gene transcription.
source: We conclude that H3K27 deacetylation likely plays a minor role in FruC-mediated fine-tuning of target gene transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: 26.7% (8788 kB / 32,939 kB) of the regions with statistically significant changes in H3K4me3 levels genome-wide displayed greater than twofold increase in fruC-null brains while 4.2% (1391 kB / 32,939 kB) of these regions showed greater than 2-fold decrease.
source: 26.7% (8788 kB / 32,939 kB) of the regions with statistically significant changes in H3K4me3 levels genome-wide displayed greater than twofold increase in fruC-null brains while 4.2% (1391 kB / 32,939 kB) of these regions showed greater than 2-fold decrease (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: 7.45% (831 kB / 11,149 kB) of FruC-bound regions showed greater than 2-fold increase in H3K4me3 in fruC-null brains.
source: 7.45% (831 kB / 11,149 kB) of FruC-bound regions showed greater than 2-fold increase in this histone mark in fruC-null brains, and these regions did not include the promoters and the bodies of Notch, dpn, and E(spl)mγ (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and G).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 5A and 5—figure supplement 1D and G.

claim: Loss of fruC function did not significantly increase the number of FruC-bound loci with greater than twofold increase in H3K4me3 comparing with the genome overall.
source: Thus, loss of fruC function did not significantly increase the number of FruC-bound loci with greater than twofold increase in H3K4me3 comparing with the genome overall.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: H3K4 demethylation unlikely plays a role in FruC-mediating fine-tuning of gene transcription.
source: We conclude that H3K4 demethylation unlikely plays a role in FruC-mediating fine-tuning of gene transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: Pc domains rarely overlapped with FruC-bound loci and did not appear to be disrupted in fruC-null brains.
source: Pc domains rarely overlapped with FruC-bound loci and did not appear to be disrupted in fruC-null brains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5B.

claim: 5.7% (1429 kB / 24,888 kB) of the regions with statistically significant changes in H3K27me3 levels displayed greater than twofold increase in fruC-null brains and 18.1% (4510 kB / 24,888 kB) of these regions showed greater than 2-fold decrease.
source: 5.7% (1429 kB / 24,888 kB) of the regions with statistically significant changes in H3K27me3 levels displayed greater than twofold increase in fruC-null brains and 18.1% (4510 kB / 24,888 kB) of these regions showed greater than 2-fold decrease (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5C.

claim: 43.3% (2748 kB / 6,340 kB) of FruC-bound regions showed greater than twofold decrease in H3K27me3 in fruC-null brains.
source: Importantly, 43.3% (2748 kB / 6,340 kB) of FruC-bound regions showed greater than twofold decrease in this histone mark in fruC-null brains (Figure 5D–E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 5D–E and 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Loss of fruC function significantly increases the number of FruC-bound loci with greater than twofold decrease in H3K27me3 comparing with the genome overall.
source: Thus, loss of fruC function significantly increases the number of FruC-bound loci with greater than twofold decrease in H3K27me3 comparing with the genome overall.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: H3K27 trimethylation likely plays an important role in FruC-mediating fine-tuning of gene transcription.
source: We conclude that H3K27 trimethylation likely plays an important role in FruC-mediating fine-tuning of gene transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: H3K27me3 levels at FruC-bound peaks including Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene loci appear significantly lower than those in Pc domains in control brains.
source: H3K27me3 levels at FruC-bound peaks including Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene loci appear significantly lower than those in Pc domains in control brains suggesting that FruC fine-tunes gene transcription by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 5A–B and 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FruC fine-tunes gene transcription by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment.
source: H3K27me3 levels at FruC-bound peaks including Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene loci appear significantly lower than those in Pc domains in control brains suggesting that FruC fine-tunes gene transcription by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: The distribution of reads throughout the genome does not appreciably change between fruC-null brains and control brains.
source: The distribution of reads throughout the genome does not appreciably change between fruC-null brains and control brains (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5F.

claim: There are many more bins that overlapped with FruC-bound peaks containing a reduced number of reads in fruC-null brains comparing with control brains.
source: Consistent with FruC promoting H3K27me3 deposition at regions bound by FruC, there are many more bins that overlapped with FruC-bound peaks containing a reduced number of reads in fruC-null brains comparing with control brains (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5F.

claim: Fruc peaks had 3-fold less coverage of H3K27me3 than canonical Pc domains.
source: We compared the coverage (reads/bp) of H3K27me3 in FruC-bound peaks to canonically defined Pc domains in neuroblasts, and found that Fruc peaks had 3-fold less coverage of H3K27me3 than canonical Pc domains (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 5G.

claim: FruC fine-tunes gene transcription by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment.
source: These results indicate that FruC fine-tunes gene transcription by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: PRC2 is thought to be the only enzymatic complex that catalyzes H3K27me3 deposition.
source: PRC2 is thought to be the only enzymatic complex that catalyzes H3K27me3 deposition (Laugesen et al., 2019; Piunti and Shilatifard, 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: FruC-bound cis-regulatory elements in Notch, dpn, and E(spl)mγ display enrichment of Su(z)12 and Caf-1.
source: We found that FruC-bound cis-regulatory elements in Notch, dpn, and E(spl)mγ display enrichment of Su(z)12 and Caf-1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 6A.

claim: Most FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts show Su(z)12 and Caf-1 enrichment.
source: Furthermore, most FruC-bound peaks in genes uniquely transcribed in type II neuroblasts show Su(z)12 and Caf-1 enrichment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 6B.

claim: Most FruC-bound peaks in genes transcribed throughout the type II neuroblast lineage also shows Su(z)12 and Caf-1 enrichment.
source: Similarly, most FruC-bound peaks in genes transcribed throughout the type II neuroblast lineage also shows Su(z)12 and Caf-1 enrichment (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 6C.

claim: FruC functions through low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment to finely tune gene transcription in type II neuroblasts.
source: These data support our model that FruC functions through low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment to finely tune gene transcription in type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CUT&RUN data.

claim: Reducing PRC2 function alone does not lead to supernumerary neuroblast formation but strongly enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains.
source: Reducing PRC2 function alone does not lead to supernumerary neuroblast formation but strongly enhances the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains, identical to the results obtained by reducing fru function (Figure 6D–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 6D–G and 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reducing PRC2 activity increases activated Notch during asymmetric neuroblast division.
source: Thus, reducing PRC2 activity increases activated Notch during asymmetric neuroblast division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: FruC functions together with PRC2 to finely tune gene expression in mitotic neuroblasts by promoting low-level enrichment of repressive histone marks in cis-regulatory elements.
source: These data led us to propose that FruC functions together with PRC2 to finely tune gene expression in mitotic neuroblasts by promoting low-level enrichment of repressive histone marks in cis-regulatory elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: FruC likely functions together with PRC2 to dampen the expression of specific genes in mitotic neuroblasts by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment at their enhancers and promoters.
source: Our data indicate that FruC likely functions together with PRC2 to dampen the expression of specific genes in mitotic neuroblasts by promoting low levels of H3K27me3 enrichment at their enhancers and promoters (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and Figure 7.

claim: Local low-level enrichment of repressive histone marks can act to fine-tune gene expression.
source: We propose that local low-level enrichment of repressive histone marks can act to fine-tune gene expression.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: Fru protein isoforms have been detected in many cell types in flies.
source: Fru protein isoforms have been detected in many cell types in flies (Ito et al., 1996; Ryner et al., 1996; Djiane et al., 2013; Michki et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021; Dillon et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: The role of Fru in stem cell differentiation remained undefined.
source: The role of Fru in stem cell differentiation remained undefined.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The identification of FruC as the sole isoform expressed in type II neuroblasts along with the use of brat-null brains has enabled the study of FruC genomic binding in a defined cell type where it is known to be expressed.
source: In this study, the identification of FruC as the sole isoform expressed in type II neuroblasts along with the use of brat-null brains, which are highly enrich for these neuroblasts, has enabled the study of FruC genomic binding in a defined cell type where it is known to be expressed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the approach used in this study.

claim: The downregulation of Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene activity by FruC correlates to PRC2-mediated low-level enrichment of H3K27me3.
source: Our data strongly correlate the downregulation of Notch and Notch downstream-effector gene activity by FruC to PRC2-mediated low-level enrichment of H3K27me3 (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and Figures 5 and 6.

claim: This mechanistic correlation appears to be broadly applicable to genes that promote stemness or prime differentiation in neuroblasts.
source: This mechanistic correlation appears to be broadly applicable to genes that promote stemness or prime differentiation in neuroblasts (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and Figures 3D and E.

claim: fru transcripts are enriched in fly renal stem cells in which Notch signaling plays an important role in regulating their stemness.
source: Transcriptomic analyses have revealed that fru transcripts are enriched in fly renal stem cells in which Notch signaling plays an important role in regulating their stemness (Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: The mechanisms described in this study might be applicable to the regulation of gene expression in the renal stem cell lineage.
source: We speculate that the mechanisms we have described in this study might be applicable to the regulation of gene expression in the renal stem cell lineage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Transcription factors Erm and Hamlet (Ham) function together with histone deacetylases to sequentially inactivate type II neuroblast functionality genes including tll and pointed during INP commitment.
source: In the type II neuroblast lineage, transcription factors Erm and Hamlet (Ham) function together with histone deacetylases to sequentially inactivate type II neuroblast functionality genes including tll and pointed during INP commitment (Weng et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2011; Eroglu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014; Koe et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2016; Hakes and Brand, 2020; Rives-Quinto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: In erm- or ham-null brains, Notch reactivation ectopically activates type II neuroblast functionality gene expression in INPs, driving their reversion into supernumerary neuroblasts.
source: In erm- or ham-null brains, Notch reactivation ectopically activates type II neuroblast functionality gene expression in INPs, driving their reversion into supernumerary neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype in erm- or ham-null brains.

claim: Mis-expressing either Erm or Ham overrides activated Notch activity in neuroblasts, and drives them to prematurely differentiate into neurons.
source: Importantly, mis-expressing either gene overrides activated Notch activity in neuroblasts, and drives them to prematurely differentiate into neurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of mis-expressing Erm or Ham.

claim: Erm- and Ham-associated histone deacetylation can robustly counteract activity of the Notch transcriptional activator complex and inactivate Notch downstream-effector gene transcription.
source: Thus, Erm- and Ham-associated histone deacetylation can robustly counteract activity of the Notch transcriptional activator complex and inactivate Notch downstream-effector gene transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the described effects of Erm and Ham.

claim: FruC appears to reduce activity of the Notch transcriptional activator complex.
source: In contrast to Erm and Ham, FruC appears to reduce activity of the Notch transcriptional activator complex instead.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Ectopic Notch activity in immature INPs due to loss of fruC function can be efficiently buffered by the multilayered gene control mechanism and does not perturb the onset of INP commitment.
source: Ectopic Notch activity in immature INPs due to loss of fruC function can be efficiently buffered by the multilayered gene control mechanism and does not perturb the onset of INP commitment (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and Figures 2F–I.

claim: Neuroblasts continually overexpressing FruC for 72 hours maintained their identities, despite displaying a reduced cell diameter and expressing markers that are typically diagnostic of Ase+ immature INPs.
source: Furthermore, neuroblasts continually overexpressing FruC for 72 hours maintained their identities, despite displaying a reduced cell diameter and expressing markers that are typically diagnostic of Ase+ immature INPs (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results and Figures 2J–L.

claim: FruC dampens rather than overrides activated Notch activity.
source: These results suggest that FruC dampens rather than overrides activated Notch activity and are consistent with the findings that FruC-bound regions displaying little changes in histone acetylation levels between fruC-null and control neuroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Transcriptional repressors that inactivate gene transcription render the activity of transcriptional activators ineffective, whereas transcriptional repressors that fine-tune gene expression dampen their activity.
source: Thus, transcriptional repressors that inactivate gene transcription render the activity of transcriptional activators ineffective, whereas transcriptional repressors that fine-tune gene expression dampen their activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Erm/Ham and FruC.

claim: FruC-bound genes in neuroblasts display undetectable levels of H3K9me3.
source: FruC-bound genes in neuroblasts display undetectable levels of H3K9me3, and knocking down hp1a function did not enhance the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in numbhypo brains (data not presented).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on experimental results.

claim: It is unlikely that FruC finely tunes gene transcription by promoting H3K9me3 enrichment.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that FruC finely tunes gene transcription by promoting H3K9me3 enrichment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: A small subset of FruC-bound peaks showed increased enrichment of H3K27ac in neuroblasts in fruC-null brains compared with control brains.
source: A small subset of FruC-bound peaks showed increased enrichment of H3K27ac in neuroblasts in fruC-null brains compared with control brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Histone deacetylation appears to play a minor role in FruC-mediated fine-tuning of gene expression in neuroblasts.
source: Thus, histone deacetylation appears to play a minor role in FruC-mediated fine-tuning of gene expression in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: PRC2 subunits and H3K27me3 are enriched in many active genes in various cell types, including embryonic stem cells and quiescent B cells in mice and human differentiating erythroid cells.
source: PRC2 subunits and H3K27me3 are enriched in many active genes in various cell types, including embryonic stem cells and quiescent B cells in mice and human differentiating erythroid cells (Brookes et al., 2012; Frangini et al., 2013; Kaneko et al., 2013; Morey et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015; Giner-Laguarda and Vidal, 2020; Ochiai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: The functional significance of PRC2 occupancies in active gene loci in vertebrate cells remains unclear due to a lack of sensitized functional readouts and a lack of insight regarding transcription factors for their recruitment.
source: However, the functional significance of their occupancies in active gene loci in vertebrate cells remains unclear due to a lack of sensitized functional readouts and a lack of insight regarding transcription factors for their recruitment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the state of knowledge in vertebrate cells.

claim: Both vertebrate and fly cells are poised to undergo a cell-state transition.
source: First, both vertebrate and fly cells are poised to undergo a cell-state transition.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a similarity between vertebrate and fly cells.

claim: The pattern of PRC2 subunit occupancy in cis-regulatory elements of active vertebrate and fly genes appears as discrete peaks that are also enriched with low levels of H3K27me3.
source: Second, the pattern of PRC2 subunit occupancy in cis-regulatory elements of active vertebrate and fly genes appears as discrete peaks that are also enriched with low levels of H3K27me3.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a similarity between vertebrate and fly genes.

claim: PRC2-mediated low-level enrichment of H3K27me3 should be broadly applicable to the fine-tuned gene activity attained by dampening transcription during binary cell fate specification and cell-state transitions in vertebrates.
source: Thus, PRC2-mediated low-level enrichment of H3K27me3 we have described in this study should be broadly applicable to the fine-tuned gene activity attained by dampening transcription during binary cell fate specification and cell-state transitions in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Loss of PRC2 activity mildly increases gene transcription levels, suggesting that PRC2 likely dampens gene transcription.
source: Studies in vertebrates have shown that loss of PRC2 activity mildly increases gene transcription levels, suggesting that PRC2 likely dampens gene transcription (Morey et al., 2013; Pherson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations.

claim: A separate study suggested a possible link between PRC2 and transcriptional bursts.
source: A separate study suggested a possible link between PRC2 and transcriptional bursts (Ochiai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: The transcriptional activator complex binding to promoters affects burst sizes, whereas their binding to enhancers control burst frequencies.
source: The transcriptional activator complex binding to promoters affects burst sizes, whereas their binding to enhancers control burst frequencies (Larsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: The dwell time of the transcriptional activator complex bound to cis-regulatory elements directly affects the frequency, duration, and amplitude of transcriptional bursts.
source: The dwell time of the transcriptional activator complex bound to cis-regulatory elements directly affects the frequency, duration, and amplitude of transcriptional bursts.
evidence: This is a direct statement about transcriptional bursts.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation and live-cell imaging of fly embryos have suggested that the Su(H) occupancy time at cis-regulatory elements of Notch downstream-effector genes increases upon Notch activation.
source: For example, chromatin immunoprecipitation and live-cell imaging of fly embryos have suggested that the Su(H) occupancy time at cis-regulatory elements of Notch downstream-effector genes increases upon Notch activation (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: Su(H)-bound regions in Notch and Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts are bound by FruC and are enriched for low levels of H3K27me3 and PRC2 subunits.
source: Our genomic data indicate that Su(H)-bound regions in Notch and Notch downstream-effector genes that promote stemness in neuroblasts are bound by FruC and are enriched for low levels of H3K27me3 and PRC2 subunits (Figures 3F–G–5A, 6A).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on CUT&RUN data and Figures 3F–G, 5A, and 6A.

claim: FruC and PRC2 might fine-tune expression of Notch pathway components by modulating transcriptional bursts in these loci.
source: These observations suggest that FruC and PRC2 might fine-tune expression of Notch pathway components by modulating transcriptional bursts in these loci.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of FruC and PRC2 function.
